1. Overarching Chiastic Structure and Old Testament Framing (Rom 10:5–13)
The Encasing Architecture: Oliver demonstrates that with the exception of verse 12 and the central confession in verses 9–10, the sub-pericope of Romans 10:5–13 consists entirely of Old Testament citations (Lev 18:5; Hab 2:4; Deut 9:4; Deut 30:12–14; Isa 28:16; Joel 2:32)

Prophetic Universal Climax (Verses 11–13): Paul concludes the passage with two prophetic citations—Isaiah 28:16 (LXX) in verse 11 (πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐπ' αὐτῷ οὐ καταισχυνθήσεται) and Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in verse 13 (πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται)—to assert that salvation is universally accessible without distinction between Jew and Greek (v. 12) [24, 26–27, 43].
Direct Quotation: "With the four statements to follow (v. 11–13), each introduced by γάρ and each supporting the previous statement, Paul asserts the universality of God’s salvation, with words or phrases such as πᾶς (vv. 11 & 13) and κύριος πάντων (v. 12)" [p. 8]

2. Textual and Hermeneutical Relationship to Deuteronomy 30:12–14 (MT & LXX)
Personification of Righteousness (Prosopopoeia): In Deuteronomy 30:11, Moses speaks directly of the commandment/Law (הַמִּצְוָה / ἐντολή), whereas in Romans 10:6a Paul personifies "the righteousness that is by faith" and introduces it with the verb λέγει ("says"), contrasting the living voice of faith with Moses writing (γράφει) in verse 5

Deliberate Omission of Obedience Clauses: Moses repeats the clause "so we/you may obey it" (καὶ ποιήσομεν αὐτό) three times in Deuteronomy 30:12, 13, and 14 [25, 27–28]. Paul systematically omits this phrase to remove the emphasis on legal works and substitute τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως ὃ κηρύσσομεν ("the word of faith that we proclaim") [24–25, 28].
Direct Quotation: "Three times Moses used the words ‘so we/you may obey it’, thereby making it clear that the Law should be obeyed... Paul does not cite these words, but implicates them in his own context" [p. 4]
11
.
Jewish Hermeneutical Technique: Oliver notes (citing Hart, Dunn, and Kruse) that Paul's method of partial quotation accompanied by interpretive glosses (τοῦτ' ἔστιν) was standard Jewish midrashic exegesis [25–26].
Direct Quotation: "The partial citation of a passage, joined by an interpretation of the words (as Paul does it here) ‘was a common Jewish approach to the exposition of an OT text’" [pp. 4–5] [25–26].
3. 'Mouth' and 'Heart' in Deuteronomy 30:14 and the Chiastic Inversion in Romans 10:9–10
Derivation from Deuteronomy 30:14: Deuteronomy 30:14 supplies the core anatomical word pair: "The word is near you; it is in your mouth (ἐν τῷ στόματί σου) and in your heart (ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου)" [24, 27–28, 35]. In Romans 10:8b, Paul attaches these terms to proclamation and faith, creating an internal 2-4-3-1 pattern: στόματι (2), καρδίᾳ (4), πίστεως (3), κηρύσσομεν (1) [58–59].
Chiastic Inversion Between Verses 9 and 10: Paul takes the 1-2-3-4 sequence in verse 9 and reverses it into a 4-3-2-1 sequence in verse 10

Distinction of Results (Righteousness vs. Salvation): Oliver refutes the claim of Ito, Dunn, and Johnson that verses 9 and 10 are synonymous poetic parallelisms [50–51]. Paul explicitly separates the bodily faculties and assigns distinct outcomes to each [38–39, 50–51, 62–63]:
Heart + Believing → results in δικαιοσύνην ("righteousness") [24, 38–39, 62].
Mouth + Confessing ("something-being-said") → results in σωτηρίαν ("salvation") [24, 38–39, 62–63].
Direct Quotation: "If then the heart and the mouth are to be distinguished, the implication is that faith and confession are also distinguished here... According to verse 10c, confession is actually not the result of salvation. The contrary, however, is true: Salvation is the result of confession" [p. 8] [50–51].
4. Theological Debate: Contrast (Moses vs. Faith) or Prophetic Testimony to Christ?
Antithesis Between Legal Works and Faith: Oliver demonstrates that Paul establishes a sharp, fundamental contrast between righteousness according to the Law (represented by Moses in v. 5 quoting Lev 18:5) and righteousness according to faith (vv. 6–10) [15–16, 30–33, 40].
Direct Quotation: "In verses 5–10 Paul describes the means of God’s salvation, contrasting verse 5 (righteousness according to the Law) with verses 6–10 (righteousness according to faith)... Verse 5 depicts the ‘old’ (Jewish) δικαιοσύνη, which is ἐκ νόμου and attached to Moses... Verse 6a brings the new δικαιοσύνη which is ἐκ πίστεως to the fore" [p. 6] [30–33].
Deuteronomy Cites a Prophetic Restoration Discourse: While Paul polemicizes against the Law, he does not treat Deuteronomy 30 as legalistic legislation; rather, he reads it as prophetic Scripture anticipating the messianic era

15
.
Direct Quotation: "This citation of Deuteronomy 30 is taken from a prophetic part of Deuteronomy where Moses prophesied about the future restoration of Israel... It seems that Paul has deliberately collected the relevant 'prophecies' to explain the situation of Israel concerning the gospel" [p. 4]
3
15
.
Synthesis: Christ Accomplished What the Law Failed to Do: Paul uses Deuteronomy 30 to show that human striving under the Law (trying to climb to heaven or plunge into the abyss) is excluded because God has already acted in Christ's incarnation and resurrection [33–35]. The remote command has been replaced by the near oral word (ῥῆμα), which calls for inward faith and outward prophetic proclamation [34–35, 65, 72–73].
Direct Quotation: "That which the righteousness (works) of the νόμος failed to accomplish, was in fact already done by God himself... This is the reason why Paul professes in verse 8 that the ῥῆμα (the spoken word) is close to his hearers – God has brought the ῥῆμα close to them through Jesus" [pp. 6–7] [34–35].

This citation of Deuteronomy 30 is taken from a prophetic part of Deuteronomy where Moses prophesied about the future restoration of Israel (cf. Ito 2006:251). In verse 11 Paul cites the prophetic words of Isaiah 28:16. The words in verse 13 are a citation from a prophecy by Joel 2:32 (as part of Jl 2:28–32).10 Paul uses these words only one more time, in 1 Corinthians 1:2, where he classifies those who call on the Name of Jesus together with the ‘church of God in Corinth’ and ‘those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be his holy people’. In this passage he is referring to Christians in general.

From these references it becomes clear that Paul is focusing on prophetic passages from the Old Testament in this sub- pericope. In the words of Ito (2006:251), ‘[i]t seems that Paul has deliberately collected the relevant “prophecies” to explain the situation of Israel concerning the gospel’. With reference to scholars like Sandnes (1991:154–171), Evans (1999:115–128) and Wagner (2002:170–176, 178–180, 356– 359), Ito (2006:251) then concluded about this action of Paul: ‘This corresponds well to his “self-portrait” as an “apostle of Gentiles” ([Romans] 11:13): he models himself after the figure of Isaiah, a prophet or herald.’ Though the first part of Ito’s quotation is good, the last part is doubtful. Although Acts 13:1 refers to Paul as a prophet and a teacher at Antioch, in his letters to the Corinthians, Romans and Galatians Paul claims the title of apostle for himself. Though the actions and lifestyle of the apostle seem to be ‘identical to those of the prophet as presented in Acts or in the classical prophetic works’ (McGinn 2000), the title of apostle, even herald or messenger, will be applied to Paul in this article as this was the way in which he presented himself. The primary function of a prophet was to proclaim the Word of God. Paul, being an apostle of Jesus, would understand that very well.
